# Summary of the Scottish National Party Manifesto 1997

## Introduction and Core Message

The 1997 SNP Manifesto, titled "Yes We Can – Win the Best for Scotland," presented a confident vision for Scottish independence under the leadership of National Convener Alex Salmond. The central message challenged both Conservative and Labour parties, arguing that Scotland's wealth had been exploited rather than supported within the UK, with £27 billion more sent to London than received since 1979.

## The Case for Independence

The manifesto outlined key facts to counter anti-independence arguments: Scotland as a wealthy nation (eighth richest when including North Sea output), automatic EU membership upon independence, open borders with England, protected pensions and investments, and full citizenship for all residents. It emphasized that over 50 countries had gained independence from Britain since 1945, with none seeking to return to colonial status.

## Route to Independence

Following election of a majority of SNP MPs, negotiations with the UK government would commence, alongside EU talks. After 6-12 months, a referendum would confirm the independence settlement, followed by formal independence declaration and fresh elections.

## Constitutional Proposals

An independent Scotland would feature a written constitution and Bill of Rights protecting basic human rights, free healthcare, education, and decent working conditions. A single-chamber parliament elected by proportional representation would be established, with voting extended to those aged 16 and over. The manifesto proposed reforming the monarchy while retaining the Queen as Head of State.

## Economic and Business Policies

The SNP promised significant tax reforms: reducing corporation tax from 33% to 30%, cutting small companies' rate from 23% to 18%, abolishing certain National Insurance contributions, and introducing banded business rates. The manifesto committed to creating 100,000 additional jobs over four years through targeted investment, export support, tourism development, and adoption of the EU Social Chapter including a minimum wage.

For personal taxation, the SNP proposed a 15% starter rate, expanded basic rate bands, and VAT reduction on domestic fuel from 8% to 5%. Approximately 85% of male and 95% of female employees would pay less tax.

## Social Policies

### Health
The manifesto proposed abolishing the internal market in the NHS, establishing independent Health Commissions, and providing £35 million additional annual funding. Dentistry would be reintegrated into the NHS, and prescription charges reformed.

### Social Justice
Measures included increasing Child Benefit to £12.50 weekly, restoring benefits for 16-17 year olds, and a "Pensioners Package" featuring £3-5 weekly pension increases, Cold Climate Allowances, and abolition of means testing for elderly care.

### Education
Priorities included hiring 700 additional teachers, upgrading school buildings, free nursery education for 3-4 year olds, replacing student loans with grants, and guaranteed internet access for schools.

### Housing
The SNP proposed transferring 75% of local authority housing debt to central government, building 20,000 socially affordable homes, and eliminating homelessness.

## Environment and Rural Scotland

Major proposals included abolishing feudal tenure, establishing a Scottish Land Commission, creating a National Forest Enterprise Board to double forest cover within 25 years, and ending nuclear reprocessing at Dounreay while developing renewable energy research.

## International Affairs

Scotland would become a full EU member with enhanced representation, join the UN, Commonwealth, and Council of Europe, and establish an Association of States of the British Isles. Defense proposals included professional Scottish Defense Forces totaling approximately 37,000 personnel, Trident removal, and eventual NATO withdrawal while maintaining European security partnerships. Overseas aid would increase to meet the 0.7% GDP UN target within six years.

## Budget and Financing

The manifesto was accompanied by a fully costed four-year budget projecting debt repayment of £6.6 billion while funding all proposed measures through Scotland's fiscal surplus with the UK, employment growth savings, and defense program changes.
